newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian race MP creates another row.
newsitem.headline: Australian race MP creates another row.

text.p: The maverick politician behind Australia's long-running racism row sparked more rowdy debate on Wednesday when she appeared on a cable television show normally reserved for lighter issues.
"You have made it creditable to be a racist in Australia," fellow panelist Lisa Wilkinson told independent MP Pauline Hanson during the taping of agony-aunt programme Beauty and the Beast.
While the show usually deals with issues such as marriage and teenage angst, Hanson's views on Asia and immigration took centre stage and prompted some angry exchanges.
"I want my sons to grow up in a country where we have open arms," said former Cleo magazine editor Wilkinson, before accusing Hanson of stoking the fires of intolerance.
Another panelist, Philippines-born Rose Hancock-Porteous, widow of mining millionaire Lang Hancock, told Hanson that she too was a proud Australian.
"Asians, what is it in us you do not like?" she said.
But Hanson, a fish-and-chip shop owner from conservative Queensland state, defended her views, saying: "I am not a redneck, I am not a racist and I won't be called one."
"It's not that I said I didn't like Asians, I said I wanted balance restored in this country."

Hanson's call in her maiden address to parliament in September for an end to immigration has struck a chord with Australian voters -- opinion polls have shown as many as two-thirds think immigration is too high.
She has, however, been blamed for a sharp rise in incidents of racist abuse and attacks in Australia.
Hanson labelled former prime minister Paul Keating a hypocrite after he described the debate on race and immigration earlier this week as "dangerously divisive".
"He has kow-towed to the Asian countries and overseas countries," said Hanson, criticising Keating's push for closer ties with Asia during his term in office.
"We were not asked. I wasn't asked if I wanted to become part of Asia... I am not part of Asia," she said.
Challenged afterwards by journalists about figures she has given on the impact of Asian immigration, Hanson said she did not believe federal Department of Immigration data.
"We've even got Asians coming in the back door through New Zealand," she said.
The panelists, meanwhile, found rather more to agree on when answering a question about whether marriage is outdated.
Twice-divorced Hanson said she was old-fashioned and still believed in marriage and the family unit.
She also felt women could make it to the top in their chosen professions: "I might be built different to a male but it doesn't mean I don't have what goes on upstairs."
